baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Uses conquest as a historical case for examining attitudes toward other societies
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: The three authored opening paragraphs of “The Morality of Conquest, ” printed 89, explicitly identify the conquest of Mexico and its texts as the case. This limited methodological connection does not assert the unread book’s full thesis or label Todorov a member of a later school.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Challenges the assumption that remembering victimhood necessarily prevents violence
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own UNESCO essay distinguishes selective remembrance from ethical use and warns that former victims can become aggressors. This is his bounded intervention on public memory, not a psychological finding or a universal judgment on victims.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Pagden adopts Todorov’s contrast between Spanish initiative and Mexica efforts to maintain the status quo in his particular interpretation of the first sustained encounter, and acknowledges Todorov’s suggestions for improving his work.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Pagden’s introduction, p. lv and note 43, explicitly identifies Todorov’s point; acknowledgments p. vi credit Todorov alongside Richard Kagan and Ángel Delgado Gómez. This is a scoped use and named feedback, not endorsement of every part of Todorov’s conquest thesis or a general claim about Indigenous passivity. Hernán Cortés is the letters’ author; Pagden is translator, editor and introduction author; J. H. Elliott’s introductory essay is separate. Pages were read in the 2001 Yale Nota Bene edition of a work first published in 1971 and revised in 1986. The witness is not backdated to 1971, and the date of each introductory revision is not independently established. Todorov’s original book and the complete letters remain unread.
